{"id": "1:5/q10", "question": "What does نَسْتَعِينُ mean and how is it formed?", "turns_on": "The derivation from ʿawn and the sense of requesting aid", "positions": [{"id": "1:5/q10/p1", "position": "Seeking help means requesting aid; the form derives from the root ʿawn with regular sound changes.", "reasons": "IBNATIYYA (author): In nastaʿīnu, the vowel of the original wāw moves to ʿayn, and the wāw becomes yāʾ because the preceding consonant has kasra. IBNATIYYA (author): The verbal noun istiʿāna derives from istiʿwānan: the wāw's vowel moves to ʿayn, then the wāw becomes alif after fatḥa. IBNATIYYA-FULL (author): Nastaʿīn derives from nastaʿūn by moving the wāw's vowel to the ʿayn and changing wāw to yāʾ after kasra. QURTUBI (author): The form nastaʿīn derives from nastaʿwinu: the vowel of wāw transfers to ʿayn and turns to yāʾ; the verbal noun derives from istaʿwana, where transferred wāw becomes alif and one of two meeting alifs is deleted, with disagreement over which, while tāʾ compensates. BAYDAWI (author): Istiʿāna is seeking help. Necessary assistance includes capacity, conceiving the act, tools, and material; when these obtain, one can be morally commanded. ABUHAYYAN (author): Istiʿāna means seeking aid; the form istifʿala has twelve uses, including request, transformation, treating something as something, and several forms of equivalence or substitution. ABUHAYYAN (author): Istiʿāna means asking for help, as in other verbs of request. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): Istiʿāna means requesting help, and requesting is one of twelve meanings of the verb pattern istifʿāl, alongside the cited related semantic functions. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): Istiʿāna is derived from the root for help, with regular vowel changes across forms, and takes either a direct object or the preposition bāʾ. ALUSI (author): The same kasra on the imperfect prefix occurs in comparable verbs such as nastaʿīnu, except where the following sound makes the kasra difficult; some also say yijillu for yajalu. {"id": "1:5/q12", "question": "For what is God's help sought?", "turns_on": "Whether the omitted object is general or restricted to worship and guidance", "positions": [{"id": "1:5/q12/p1", "position": "The request is general, including worship and every affair.", "reasons": "KASHSHAF (author): Seeking help is unqualified so it covers every matter in which help is needed. TABRISI (author): Nastaʿīn means asking God for success and assistance in worship and all affairs; tawfiq combines all causes needed for an act to occur. NASAFI (author): The unqualified request for aid embraces every kind of help; alternatively, it asks God’s help and enabling for worship, with ‘guide us’ specifying the requested assistance. NASAFI-FULL (author): The request for aid is unrestricted and covers every need; alternatively it asks for God's help and enabling grace in performing acts of worship, which the following request for guidance specifies. ABUHAYYAN (author): The unqualified terms worship and seeking help encompass every act of worship and every matter for which help is sought. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): Both worship and seeking help are unqualified so they include every act of worship and every matter for which help is sought. IBNKATHIR (ابن عباس): Ibn Abbas says the servant worships, fears, and hopes in God alone, and seeks His help for obedience and every affair. DURR (ابن عباس): Ibn Abbas says the servant seeks God's help for obedience and for all affairs. DURR-FULL (ابن عباس): Ibn Abbas explains “You alone we worship” as worshipping, affirming God's oneness, fearing and hoping in Him alone, and seeking His help for obedience and all affairs. ITQAN (author): An omitted complement can express generality: 'You alone we ask for help' means in worship and all our affairs, while God's call to the Abode of Peace addresses each person. ALUSI (author): The unexpressed object of seeking aid may be unrestricted, like an omitted object that implies generality; choosing only some needs would require an arbitrary preference. ALUSI (البيضاوي): Al-Ālūsī says al-Bayḍāwī’s presentation also points toward preferring an unrestricted object of aid. ALUSI (author): Al-Ālūsī nevertheless prefers the unrestricted sense: seeking aid through worship can serve every legitimate purpose, and the straight path embraces all religious and worldly affairs and ultimate salvation. ALUSI (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم): In an authentic report, the Prophet tells Ibn ʿAbbās: when you seek aid, seek it from God; al-Ālūsī sees this as supporting unrestricted reliance and thinks it likely explains Ibn ʿAbbās’s view of the verse. ALUSI-FULL (بعضهم): Some take the unexpressed object of seeking help universally, like an unrestricted verb of giving; al-Bayḍāwī's practice favors this, and it accords with a report from Ibn ʿAbbās. {"id": "1:5/q13", "question": "What kinds of divine aid does the request concern?", "turns_on": "Whether ability and aid precede, accompany, or facilitate action", "positions": [{"id": "1:5/q13/p1", "position": "Aid includes the capacity and conditions necessary for action.", "reasons": "TABRISI (author): A second reason to ask is to retain capacity for future obedience over time or to avoid acts that would cancel capacity, depending on one's theory of its persistence. RAZI-FULL (author): Human capacity is equally disposed to acting or abstaining; action needs a preponderating motive, which cannot come from the servant without regress, so God must assist. RAZI-FULL (author): People with similar ability, intellect, effort, and desire seek true belief, yet only some attain it; the needed aid must come from God rather than a human or angel, which would restart the question. RAZI-FULL (author): Rāzī resolves the dispute by saying capacity affects action only alongside a decisive motive; divine assistance creates that motive and removes the contrary one. RAZI-FULL (author): God's share is creating the decisive motive; the servant's share is that the action issues from him when capacity and motive coincide, a subtle account of agency. ITQAN (قيل): A spiritual explanation sees a movement from creatures’ initial distance and inability to converse with God to readiness for intimate address after knowing, praising, and worshipping Him. ALUSI (author): If the verse bears on created acts, al-Ālūsī takes it to affirm that people have real capacity to act, effective by God’s permission but not independent of Him. ALUSI (author): Al-Ālūsī says the worship clause presupposes an effective human capacity: one cannot be told to produce an act without some capacity that contributes to its occurrence; kasb alone does not satisfy him. ALUSI-FULL (author): Iyyaka nastaʿīn denies independence: human capacity and action depend on God's permission and aid, yielding neither compulsion nor delegation of control. ELMALILI (author): In voluntary acts we are the proximate cause through our request, but not the complete cause, since we depend on necessary aid; the Creator makes the total causal set. IBNASHUR (العلماء): Scholars define necessary aid as creating what completes an act: the agent’s capacity, awareness of the act, its material, and its tool; together these are ability or sound means and tools, enabling moral obligation. IBNASHUR (الراغب): Al-Raghib calls the second, easing kind of aid tawfīq; the author says this does not conflict with scholars’ definition because it follows the necessary aid that first makes tawfīq possible. SAMARRAI-LAMASAT (author): Worship is impossible without God’s aid and enabling; seeking aid admits human inability and dependence, countering pride and arrogance. SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT (author): Worship is possible only with God's aid and enabling; asking for help cures pride and admits human weakness and inability to bear the trust unaided."}, {"id": "1:5/q13/p2", "position": "God's enabling aid accompanies and sustains action.", "reasons": "KASHSHAF (author): Best is asking God and His enabling grace for help in worship; 1:6 specifies aid as guidance.
